title: CI/CD Pipelines
subtitle: Follow one small commit through build, test, artifact and deploy stages, then watch a bad release get rolled back.
learn: What each pipeline stage (build, test, artifact, deploy) is for and why the order matters
Why trunk-based development pairs with small, frequent merges
Why you build one artifact once and promote that same artifact to every environment
How pipeline-as-code makes delivery reviewable and repeatable
How rollback works and why it should be the fastest thing your pipeline does

steps.title: How does code reach users?
steps.body: A developer finishes a 40-line change. Old-style teams batch changes for weeks, then hand a release to an ops team and hope. A CI/CD pipeline replaces that hope with a fixed, automated path from commit to production. Continuous integration means merging often and checking every merge. Continuous delivery means every passing merge is ready to ship.
steps.idea: A pipeline turns 'ship it' from a risky event into a boring, repeatable routine.
steps.caption: One small change is ready to leave the laptop.

steps.title: Merge small, merge often
steps.body: In trunk-based development everyone merges into one main branch at least daily. Branches live hours, not weeks, so they rarely diverge and merge conflicts stay tiny. Unfinished work is hidden behind a feature flag instead of a long-lived branch. Each push to main triggers the pipeline through a webhook.
steps.idea: Small changes are easier to review, to test and to undo, so trunk-based development makes everything downstream cheaper.
steps.caption: Push lands on main and fires a webhook.

steps.title: Build in a clean runner
steps.body: The CI runner checks out the exact commit on a fresh machine, restores cached dependencies, and compiles the code. A clean environment catches 'works on my laptop' bugs such as an undeclared dependency. Fast steps run first: linting and compiling fail in seconds, so a typo never waits behind a 10-minute suite. With caching, a typical build takes about 2 minutes.
steps.idea: Build in a clean, pinned environment so the result depends only on the commit.
steps.caption: Runner compiles commit a1b2c3d from scratch.

steps.title: Run the gates
steps.body: Unit tests run first because they are fast and cheap, then integration tests, then security and dependency scans. Any failure stops the pipeline and blocks the change from going further. Say 1,240 tests pass in about 6 minutes by running in parallel across several runners. Keep this stage under roughly 10 minutes, or people stop waiting for it. How to design the tests themselves is covered in the testing lesson.
steps.idea: Order stages cheapest-first and fail fast, so feedback arrives in minutes.
steps.caption: All 1,240 tests pass in parallel shards.

steps.title: Package once, store it
steps.body: Now CI builds one immutable artifact, for example a container image, and tags it with the commit SHA, such as shop-api:a1b2c3d. It is pushed to an artifact registry. From here on, every environment runs this exact image and never rebuilds. Rebuilding per environment could pull in different dependency versions, so what you tested would not be what you shipped.
steps.idea: Build once, promote the same artifact everywhere; only configuration differs between environments.
steps.caption: Image shop-api:a1b2c3d is stored in the registry.

steps.title: Staging, then production
steps.body: The pipeline first deploys the image to staging, a production-like environment, and runs smoke tests: log in, load a page, place a test order. If they pass, the same image is promoted to production, automatically (continuous deployment) or after a human approval (continuous delivery). The pipeline definition lives in the repo as code, a YAML file reviewed like any other change, so the process itself is versioned. Rollout strategies such as canary are covered in the deploys lesson.
steps.idea: Pipeline as code makes the delivery process reviewable, versioned and identical on every run.
steps.caption: Same image runs in staging, then production.

steps.title: The release is bad
steps.body: Suppose the change passed every test but has a bug that only real traffic exposes, and the error rate climbs from 0.2% to 6%. Tests cannot catch everything, which is why production monitoring is part of the pipeline's feedback loop. A fix-forward patch would take at least another 20 minutes of pipeline time while customers keep failing. Observability is its own lesson; here the point is that something has to trigger the next move.
steps.idea: Passing tests means 'probably fine'; production signals decide whether it really is.
steps.caption: Errors in production jump to 6%.

steps.title: Redeploy the last good image
steps.body: Because the registry still holds the previous artifact, a rollback is just a deploy of shop-api:9f8e7d6, with no rebuild and no new tests. It can finish in about a minute. This works only if old artifacts are kept and the release was backward compatible with the data it touched; a one-way database change makes rollback unsafe, and that is why expand/contract migrations exist. Rolling back first, then debugging calmly, is the standard habit.
steps.idea: Rollback should be a one-click redeploy of a stored artifact, faster than any fix-forward.
steps.caption: Production pulls the previous image; errors fall.

steps.title: The path from commit to users
steps.body: Merge small changes to trunk often. The pipeline builds in a clean runner, runs tests cheapest-first, packages one immutable artifact, and promotes that artifact through staging to production. The pipeline is code in the repo. When production signals go bad, redeploy the previous artifact first and investigate second.
steps.idea: Small changes, one artifact, automated gates, and a fast way back.
steps.caption: Commit to production in about 14 minutes.

quiz.q: Staging passed all smoke tests, but the pipeline then rebuilds the code from source for production. What is the main risk?
options: Production will be slower to start
The production build may differ from what was tested, for example through newer dependency versions
Staging data will leak into production
The registry will run out of space
quiz.why: Rebuilding creates a new artifact that was never tested. Building once and promoting the same image guarantees production runs exactly what staging validated.

quiz.q: Your pipeline runs a 25-minute end-to-end suite before the 30-second lint check. What is the best change?
options: Remove the lint check
Run the slow suite on a nightly schedule only
Skip tests on small changes
Run lint and unit tests first to fail fast, and parallelise or trim the slow suite
quiz.why: Cheapest-first ordering gives quick failure feedback. Slow suites should be sharded in parallel or moved later, not skipped.

quiz.q: A team keeps feature branches open for three weeks, then merges. Which problem does trunk-based development mainly address?
options: Slow network speed to the registry
Missing database indexes
Large, conflict-prone merges and big risky releases
Too many environments
quiz.why: Long-lived branches diverge, causing painful merges and large untested batches. Merging small changes daily keeps integration cheap and each release small.

quiz.q: A release raises production errors to 6%. The previous image is still in the registry. What is usually the best first move?
options: Write and ship a fix through the full pipeline
Redeploy the previous artifact, then investigate
Delete the failing tests
Rebuild the old commit from source
quiz.why: Redeploying a stored, known-good artifact restores service in about a minute. Fix-forward takes a full pipeline run while users keep failing.

quiz.q: When might rolling back the application image NOT be enough to undo a release?
options: When the image was tagged with a commit SHA
When staging is down
When tests ran in parallel
When the release also ran a one-way database migration that the old code cannot work with
quiz.why: Code rolls back easily, but data changes do not. Backward-compatible, expand/contract migrations keep the old version working against the new schema.

cheatsheet.def: Merge to a shared main branch often, and automatically build and test every merge.
Delivery: every passing change is ready to ship, release is a button. Deployment: it ships to production automatically.
Everyone merges to main at least daily; unfinished work hides behind feature flags, not long branches.
A versioned build output (image, package) tagged by commit SHA, built once and promoted unchanged through environments.
The pipeline definition (YAML) lives in the repo, so it is reviewed, versioned and reproducible.
Order stages cheapest-first (lint, unit, integration, e2e) so most failures show up within minutes.
Redeploy the previous known-good artifact. Needs retained artifacts and backward-compatible data changes.
Aim for under 10 minutes from commit to test result, and a rollback under a few minutes.
